title: The Sinner You Look Down On May Be Closer to Repentance Than the Christian Who Thinks He Has Nothing to Confess
paragraphs: The Sinner You Look Down On May Be Closer to Repentance Than the Christian Who Thinks He Has Nothing to Confess

The frightening lesson of Jesus’ parable is not that obvious sinners are beyond grace. It is that a person can stand in a place of prayer, speak religious words, live a respectable life—and still be unable to see how desperately he needs mercy.
There were two men standing before God.
One looked like he belonged there.
The other probably wished he could disappear.
One had the vocabulary of religion, the discipline of religion, the reputation of religion.
The other had a reputation he could not hide.
And if you had been standing outside the temple that day, watching them walk in, you might have guessed which man God would approve.
You might have been completely wrong.
That is what makes Luke 18:10–14 so uncomfortable.

Jesus tells us about a Pharisee and a tax collector who went to the temple to pray. The Pharisee represented religious seriousness. The tax collector belonged to a profession widely associated in that setting with collaboration, exploitation, and moral disgrace.
One man could point to his religious achievements.
The other could barely lift his eyes.
Yet Jesus says it was the broken sinner who went home justified.
Not the religious man.
And before we turn the Pharisee into another villain we can comfortably condemn, we should notice the trap.
The moment we say, “Thank God I’m not self-righteous like that Pharisee,” we may already be praying his prayer.
Jesus introduces the parable with words sharp enough to expose an entire religious instinct:
“He also told this parable to some who trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and treated others with contempt.”
Luke 18:9.
The Greek is even more revealing.
The phrase translated “trusted in themselves” contains the words πεποιθότας ἐφ’ ἑαυτοῖς—pepoithotas eph’ heautois.
Their confidence had settled upon themselves.
That was the disease beneath everything else.

They were not merely people who wanted to obey God. Scripture does not condemn sincere obedience. Jesus was confronting people whose confidence before God rested in what they believed themselves to be.
And that inward confidence produced an outward consequence.
Luke says they treated others with contempt.
The Greek uses ἐξουθενοῦντας—exouthenountas—carrying the sense of despising, regarding as insignificant, treating someone as though they were of little account.
Self-righteousness rarely stays inside the heart.
Eventually, it changes the way you look at people.
Especially sinful people.
Especially messy people.
Especially people whose failures are easier to see than yours.
Jesus continues:
“Two men went up into the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector.”
Both entered the same temple.
Both approached the same God.
Both prayed.
But only one understood why he needed to be there.
The Pharisee stood and prayed:
“God, I thank you that I am not like other men…”
Then came the comparisons.
Extortioners.
Unjust.
Adulterers.
And finally:
“…or even like this tax collector.”
Imagine hearing that while standing nearby.
Imagine being the tax collector.
You came into the temple carrying enough shame already, and somewhere near you is a religious man using your broken life as evidence of his own righteousness.
But listen carefully to the Pharisee.
He begins with God.
He says thank you.
He talks about fasting.
He talks about giving.
He sounds spiritual.
That is precisely why this parable is dangerous.
Self-righteousness does not always sound arrogant.
Sometimes it sounds like testimony.
Sometimes it sounds like discernment.
Sometimes it quotes Scripture.
Sometimes it talks about holiness.
Sometimes it posts Christian content.
Sometimes it serves at church.
Sometimes it gives money.
Sometimes it fasts.
Sometimes it can identify everything wrong with the culture while remaining almost completely incapable of saying:
“Lord, something is wrong with me.”
There is nothing wrong with fasting.
There is nothing wrong with giving.
There is nothing wrong with refusing adultery, injustice, exploitation, or immorality.
The problem was not that the Pharisee practiced moral disciplines.
The problem was what he had made those disciplines mean.
His obedience had become evidence in a case he was building for himself.
And the tax collector became the comparison that made the case feel convincing.
That temptation is still alive.
“I would never cheat on my spouse.”
“I don’t drink like they do.”
“I’m not sexually immoral like them.”
“I know my Bible.”
“I attend church.”
“I tithe.”
“I serve.”
“I don’t believe what those people believe.”
“I’m not like that denomination.”
“I’m not like those hypocrites.”
“I’m not like those addicts.”
“I’m not like those people online.”
“I’m not like him.”
“I’m not like her.”
And hidden underneath all of it can be the same ancient prayer:
“God, thank You that I am not like them.”
Maybe you have never spoken those words.
Maybe your heart has.
Then Jesus moves our attention across the temple.
There stands the tax collector.
“But the tax collector, standing far off, would not even lift up his eyes to heaven…”
No résumé.
No comparison.
No defense.
No explanation of how difficult his childhood was.
No list of people worse than him.
No attempt to negotiate with God.
Jesus says he beat his breast and prayed:
“God, be merciful to me, a sinner!”
The Greek is devastatingly beautiful:
Ὁ θεός, ἱλάσθητί μοι τῷ ἁμαρτωλῷ.
Ho Theos, hilastheti moi tō hamartōlō.
“God, be merciful to me, the sinner.”
The crucial word is ἱλάσθητί—hilastheti.
This is more than a casual request for God to overlook a mistake. The word belongs to the biblical world of atonement and propitiation. The man knows he cannot manufacture the righteousness he needs.
He needs mercy from God.
He has stopped presenting evidence for his goodness.
He has started pleading for grace.
And Jesus says:
“I tell you, this man went down to his house justified, rather than the other.”
Justified.
The Greek verb is δεδικαιωμένος—dedikaiōmenos.
The disgraced man went home having been declared righteous before God.
Think about the scandal of that sentence.
Jesus does not say the tax collector's sin did not matter.
He does not call evil good.
He does not tell us repentance means continuing comfortably in rebellion.
Grace never requires God to pretend sin is harmless.
The Gospel is infinitely better than that.
God takes sin so seriously that forgiveness ultimately leads us to a cross.
Jesus Christ would bear sin.
The innocent for the guilty.
The righteous for the unrighteous.
The spotless Lamb for sinners who could never wash themselves clean.
The tax collector's prayer points toward the very thing every sinner needs:
atoning mercy that we cannot provide for ourselves.
This is why Christianity is not ultimately the story of good people climbing high enough to reach God.
It is the story of God coming down to rescue sinners.
And that means the person you quietly consider beneath you may, at this very moment, be spiritually closer to the posture Jesus commends than you are.
That addict you judge.
That woman whose past everyone knows.
That man who destroyed his marriage.
That teenager who walked away from church.
That prisoner.
That alcoholic.
That skeptic.
That person whose language makes you uncomfortable.
That person whose political opinions make you angry.
That person whose sexual sin is visible while yours remains hidden.
That person sitting at the back of the church hoping nobody recognizes them.
That person who has not entered a church building in twenty years because the last Christians they met made them feel like contamination.
Do not misunderstand this.
Their sin is real.
So is yours.
The Gospel does not erase the distinction between righteousness and wickedness.
It destroys our illusion that we can stand before a holy God on the basis of our superiority to another sinner.
You can be correct about somebody else's sin and still be terribly wrong about your own heart.
You can win an argument about morality and lose sight of mercy.
You can defend biblical truth and secretly enjoy feeling superior to the people who violate it.
You can hate the darkness in the world while protecting the darkness in yourself.
You can become so skilled at identifying everybody else's compromise that you forget how to confess your own.
And perhaps the most terrifying possibility of all:
You can become accustomed to talking about Jesus without being astonished that you personally need His blood.
The Pharisee's tragedy was not simply that he noticed sin.
Jesus noticed sin.
The apostles confronted sin.
The prophets confronted sin.
Biblical love does not require moral blindness.
The Pharisee's tragedy was that another man's sin had become a mirror in which he admired himself.
There is a difference between grieving someone's sin and needing their sin to make you feel righteous.
There is a difference between saying, “That road leads to destruction,” and secretly whispering, “Their destruction proves I am better.”
There is a difference between holiness and superiority.
Jesus calls us to holiness.
Pride manufactures superiority.
And pride is extraordinarily difficult to diagnose because it can feed on good things.
Bible knowledge can feed it.
Theology can feed it.
Ministry can feed it.
Giving can feed it.
Fasting can feed it.
Years of church attendance can feed it.
Even repentance can become something we boast about if we begin looking down upon people who have not yet reached the place where grace brought us.
That is why the Gospel keeps bringing us back to the foot of the cross.
There, boasting dies.
There, the successful businessman and the homeless addict need the same Savior.
The pastor and the prostitute need the same blood.
The lifelong church member and the convicted criminal need the same mercy.
The scholar and the skeptic must enter through the same Door.
There are not two crosses.
There is not one cross for respectable sinners and another for scandalous ones.
There is Jesus.
Only Jesus.
Paul writes in Romans 3:23:
All.
Then comes grace.
Those who are justified are justified by God's grace as a gift through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.
That means your worst sin does not place you beyond the reach of Christ when you come to Him in repentance and faith.
And your best religious performance does not place you beyond the need for Christ.
Read that again.
Your worst sin does not make Jesus too small to save you.
Your best behavior does not make you too good to need saving.
That is the scandal of grace.
Some people will hate it because they want Christianity to confirm that they are better than the people they despise.
Others will misunderstand it because they think grace means sin no longer matters.
The cross destroys both illusions.
At Calvary, we discover that sin is worse than we wanted to admit.
And grace is greater than we dared to imagine.
Your sin was serious enough that the Son of God went willingly to the cross.
His mercy is powerful enough that the repentant sinner does not have to remain imprisoned by what he has done.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Peter denied Jesus.
Grace restored him.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Grace transformed him into an apostle.
The thief crucified beside Jesus could offer Christ no decades of religious achievement, no opportunity to rebuild his reputation, no impressive ministry record.
He could only turn toward Jesus.
And Jesus promised him paradise.
Again and again, Scripture refuses to let a person's worst chapter have authority over the ending once Jesus enters the story.
But there is something grace will not permit you to keep.
Your throne.
You cannot cling to self-righteousness and simultaneously boast in Christ as though both were responsible for your salvation.
Eventually, one has to fall.
Either Jesus becomes your righteousness…
or you continue trying to manufacture your own.
Maybe that is why this parable bothers you.
Maybe you expected to read about somebody else.
Maybe a name came into your mind while you were reading.
Someone you think needs this article.
Someone proud.
Someone hypocritical.
Someone religious.
Someone judgmental.
Maybe you were already preparing to send it to them.
Send it if God leads you.
But before you do, ask the harder question:
“Jesus… where am I in this story?”
Not your spouse.
Not your pastor.
Not your parents.
Not your church.
Not that person on Facebook.
You.
When was the last time you confessed sin without immediately explaining why you did it?
When was the last time you asked God to search you instead of asking Him to fix everybody around you?
When was the last time another person's failure produced grief in you instead of secret satisfaction?
When was the last time you looked at someone trapped in sin and remembered:
“But for the mercy of Christ, I have nothing to boast about either”?
Perhaps you have been hiding behind Christian activity.
You know the songs.
You know when to say amen.
You know Scripture.
People may even come to you for spiritual advice.
But somewhere along the road, confession became rare.
Not because you stopped sinning.
Because you became better at noticing everybody else's.
If that sentence hurts, do not run from it.
Conviction can be mercy.
Jesus did not tell this parable because He enjoys humiliating religious people.
He told it because self-righteousness can keep a person from recognizing his need for grace.
And Jesus loves sinners enough to expose whatever keeps us from coming to Him.
Maybe you are reading this from the opposite side.
You are the person people whisper about.
Your past follows you into rooms.
You made choices you cannot undo.
You hurt people.
Maybe you have been sexually immoral.
Maybe addiction hollowed out years of your life.
Maybe you abandoned your family.
Maybe you lied.
Maybe you betrayed somebody.
Maybe you walked away from God.
Maybe church people know just enough of your story to make you feel permanently disqualified.
Listen carefully.
Jesus did not praise the tax collector's sin.
He received the sinner who knew he needed mercy.
There is an enormous difference.
You do not have to pretend your sin was small.
You do not have to rewrite your past before Jesus can rewrite your future.
Bring Him the truth.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the consequences.
Bring Him the secret you have spent years hiding.
Bring Him the version of yourself you cannot stand looking at anymore.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Come to Christ.
First John 1:9 tells believers that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
The answer to shame is not pretending you never sinned.
The answer is Jesus Christ.
And if you are the religious person who suddenly recognizes yourself in the Pharisee, the answer is also Jesus Christ.
There is grace for the self-righteous too.
That may be one of the most beautiful truths hidden inside this uncomfortable story.
The Pharisee needed mercy just as desperately as the tax collector.
And so do we.
So stop measuring your righteousness against somebody else's wreckage.
The standard was never your neighbor.
The standard is the holiness of God.
And when that truth finally breaks our pride, we stop asking:
“Am I better than them?”
We start praying:
“God, have mercy on me.”
That prayer changes the way you see everybody.
Suddenly, the person you used to condemn becomes someone you pray for.
The prodigal becomes someone you hope comes home.
The addict becomes someone worth sitting beside.
The skeptic becomes someone worth listening to.
The hypocrite becomes someone you confront with tears rather than contempt.
The broken become people you no longer discuss merely as problems.
You remember they are people for whom Christ died.
And you remember that you live by mercy too.
This does not weaken truth.
It makes truth look more like Jesus.
Full of grace and truth.
Not grace without truth.
Not truth without grace.
Jesus Christ.
Maybe our churches would look different if we remembered this.
Maybe our comment sections would look different.
Maybe our marriages would look different.
Maybe Christians would become known not as people who pretend sin does not exist, nor as people who enjoy condemning sinners, but as people who understand exactly where sinners can find forgiveness.
At the cross.
At the feet of Jesus.
There is room there for the tax collector.
There is room there for the Pharisee who finally realizes he is not as righteous as he thought.
There is room there for you.
And there is room there for me.
But we come empty-handed.
No comparison.
No spiritual résumé.
No list of people worse than us.
Only repentance.
Only faith.
Only mercy.
Only Christ.
So before you leave this article and return to the noise of your day, sit with the question Jesus' parable refuses to let us escape:
When you stand before God, what are you trusting in?
Your morality?
Your church attendance?
Your theology?
Your generosity?
Your reputation?
The fact that you have never committed the sins that ruined somebody else's life?
Or Jesus Christ?
Because the sinner you look down on may already be beating his chest somewhere, whispering through tears:
“God, have mercy on me.”
While the person convinced he has nothing to confess may still be talking about everyone except himself.
If this exposed something hidden in you, do not perform spirituality here.
Be honest.
Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that Jesus still restores people.
Then think of one person who needs this message.
Not somebody you want to shame.
Somebody you love.
There may come a day when somebody else's failure tempts you to feel superior.
Read it again then.
Never forget this:
The safest place for a sinner is not pretending he has no scandal—it is kneeling before the Savior whose grace can write an ending his sin never could.
